title: Functional Divergence Between the Two Cerebral Hemispheres Contributes to Human Fluid Intelligence
summary: Researchers studied 777 people and found that the more the two brain hemispheres function differently from each other — particularly in the frontoparietal network, which governs problem-solving and flexible thinking — the higher a person's fluid intelligence. It's not that one side is 'dominant,' but rather that the gap between what each side does well is what drives smarter thinking. This asymmetry also appears to be an evolutionary trait: the greater the hemispheric divergence, the more it tracks with how much the human cortex has expanded compared to other primates.
takeaway: The brain gets smarter when its two hemispheres diverge — not when they agree. I keep thinking about this in the context of design: diversity, empathy, and the hard work of decoding each other's perspective might be the human equivalent of that same mechanism. When diverse thinking grows from one person, empathy sprouts.

title: Longitudinal Changes in Brain Asymmetry Track Lifestyle and Disease
summary: Your brain's left-right balance isn't fixed — it shifts over your lifetime based on your lifestyle and health. Using data from 1,425 people, researchers found that things like retirement, daily habits, and diseases measurably change how asymmetric your brain is. The left and right hemispheres handle different jobs, and shifts in their balance connect to thousands of health outcomes.
takeaway: People aren't static. The mental models users bring to your product today are shaped by everything they've lived through. Design for the person who is always changing, not a fixed archetype.

title: Developing brain asymmetry shapes cognitive and psychiatric outcomes in adolescence
summary: Researchers tracked over 11,000 adolescents aged 10–14 and found that the brain's left and right hemispheres develop asymmetrically in predictable ways — the left frontotemporal regions expand while the right parietal and occipital areas grow. These asymmetry patterns were linked to crystallized intelligence (accumulated knowledge and skills) and early-onset mental health risks. Early-life health and genetic factors related to synapse formation shaped how this asymmetry developed, suggesting the brain's unevenness is an adaptive feature that supports specialized thinking.
takeaway: If the brain is literally building its knowledge architecture between ages 10–14, then products for teens shouldn't just deliver content — they should accumulate with the user. Crystallized intelligence is about compounding knowledge and experience over time. Products that mirror that — where your history, progress, and insights grow richer the longer you stay — aren't just sticky. They're aligned with how the brain actually develops. That's where education and mental health products have a massive untapped advantage.

title: Building compositional tasks with shared neural subspaces
summary: Princeton neuroscientists found that the prefrontal cortex stores reusable patterns of neural activity — 'cognitive Legos' — that the brain snaps together to perform new tasks. Instead of learning each skill from scratch, it grabs an existing block (e.g., 'discriminate color') and wires its output into another ('drive an action'), composing complex behavior from small, pre-trained parts. Unused blocks are actively suppressed. This modular compositionality appears unique to the prefrontal cortex, and it's a trick AI systems haven't yet mastered.
takeaway: Good B2C onboarding isn't teaching — it's triggering the cognitive block the user already has, which is probably why tropes never die.

title: Chunking as a rational strategy for optimizing working memory
summary: Brown University researchers built a computer model of the brain regions responsible for working memory (basal ganglia and thalamus) and discovered that our memory limits aren't really about storage capacity — they're about learning. The brain has learned to strategically 'chunk' related pieces of information together (like grouping shades of blue) to conserve mental space, and dopamine acts as the reward signal that reinforces this chunking strategy. When the model was given unlimited storage but no chunking ability, it actually performed worse — meaning the limit isn't a bug, it's a feature that forces the brain to find smarter organizing patterns. The findings also explain why people with dopamine-related conditions (Parkinson's, ADHD, schizophrenia) struggle with working memory differently.
takeaway: A smart, smaller home makes you happier than a giant disorganized one — but you only feel that truth after living in it. The design challenge is making people sense it at the moment of choosing, because 'less but better' is a luxury people will pay more for.
